Solidarity Association (UniKuir) and Advocates for Human Rights. 46 Submissions by Angaza Foundation, Pyali Chatterjee and others, Coming Out, ILGA World, Single Step Foundation and others. 47 Submissions by Coming Out, HRAU Timor-Leste, Santa Marta Centre and others. 48 Submissions by Coming Out, Save the Children Thailand and others. 49 Submission by Outright International and others. 50 Submissions by Qun Jelesi, Coming Out, Outright International and others. 10/21 and inclusive education.51 As a result, many LGBT learners conceal their identities until university or beyond, fearing harm or academic repercussions. 52
committee: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity
committees: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity

text: A positive example of an LGBT-inclusive protection mechanism at the university level is the Discrimination and Violence Prevention Unit at Özyeğin University in Türkiye. The unit actively engages with the LGBT student club, organizes events and provides counselling and guidance tailored to the needs of LGBT students, thereby contributing to a more inclusive and supportive campus environment.53 Similarly, in the Philippines, some higher education institutions have independently implemented progressive practices to support LGBT students, including gender-sensitive mental health support systems, facilitated by trained counsellors, institutional partnerships with gender studies centres and LGBT student organizations.54 C. Enforcement of strict binary gender norms
committee: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity
committees: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity

text: In many States, there are no laws or policies that protect students’ right to express their gender identity in school settings, including through dress. 55 The enforcement of strict binary gender norms and restrictions on diverse gender expression contributes to hostile and exclusionary educational environments and violates learners’ rights to freedom of expression. These restrictions also adversely affect students who are perceived to be LGBT based on their appearance or mannerisms. Schools in all regions may impose rigid and gendered standards for student appearance – such as uniforms, hairstyles or grooming – that lack any pedagogical justification. Such policies disproportionately impact transgender and gender nonconforming students, compelling them to suppress their identities in order to conform, often at significant personal and psychological cost.
committee: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity
committees: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity

text: Schools may impose compulsory male and female uniforms, enforce gendered dress codes even in the absence of uniforms and establish gender-specific rules regarding haircuts, makeup, personal belongings such as school bags, or even expected patterns of speech and social interaction deemed “masculine” or “feminine”.56 In some cases, students have been subjected to forced haircuts by school staff.57 Learners may also be prohibited from participating in graduation ceremonies or end-of-year celebrations in attire that aligns with their gender identity, depriving them of full participation in significant social milestones.58 Requiring LGBT students to dress in ways that contradict their identity compels them to hide who they are, suppress their authentic expression and conform to discriminatory expectations. These requirements not only undermine their dignity but also distract from academic engagement and contribute to psychosocial distress, often causing emotional exhaustion. As a positive example, universities in Thailand have adopted policies that allow students of all gender identities to wear clothing of their choice during entrance exams, in classrooms and at graduation ceremonies.59 51 Submissions by RSFL Ungdom, Human Rights Watch and Young Pride Foundation. 52 Submission by Sarajevo Open Centre. 53 Submission by UniKuir and Advocates for Human Rights. 54 Submission by Commission on Human Rights of the Philippines. 55 Submission by Pyali Chatterjee and others. 56 Submissions by anonymous civil society organization, Angaza Foundation, Comisión de Derechos Humanos de la Ciudad de México, Commission on Human Rights of the Philippines, Save the Children Thailand and others, and joint report by Certified NPO ReBit, Tnet, Proud Futures and General Incorporated Association Niji-zu. 57 Submission by Young Pride Foundation. 58 Submission by Háttér Society. 59 Submissions by Save the Children Thailand and Young Pride Foundation. D. Specific forms of discrimination and harms for transgender and gender-diverse learners
committee: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity
committees: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity

text: Transgender and gender-diverse students face additional and specific forms of discrimination within educational settings. They frequently face prohibitions or restrictions on accessing facilities that align with their gender identity, including bathrooms, dormitories and other sex-segregated spaces. 60 Gender-neutral facilities remain uncommon in most educational institutions. As a result, transgender and genderdiverse students are often compelled to use facilities that conflict with their gender identity, which exposes them to heightened risks of discrimination, harassment and emotional distress. The lack of inclusive facilities undermines students’ safety, dignity and ability to participate fully in school life. There are some efforts to address these concerns. For example, some schools in the Philippines have introduced inclusive or all-gender restrooms to promote safer and more inclusive environments for students.61
committee: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity
committees: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity

text: Organized sports are predominantly structured along binary gender lines, and transgender and gender-diverse learners often face blanket exclusions from participation. While some States and institutions allow participation in teams aligned with a student’s gender identity, such efforts remain inconsistent and limited. 62 Bullying and harassment of transgender and gender nonconforming students in sports settings is widespread in many contexts, contributing to a hostile environment. 63 As a result, transgender and gender-diverse learners avoid participating in sports altogether. Whether by prohibition or opting out, these learners are deprived of their right to participate in sport and miss out on the physical, social and developmental benefits of athletic engagement.64
committee: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity
committees: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity

text: Laws that deny the possibility of legal recognition, including for children, of self-defined gender identity – or that allow such recognition only under restrictive conditions, such as undergoing medical transition – are discriminatory and violate the right to identity.65 Legal gender recognition enables individuals to change their name and gender marker on official documents, including birth certificates, passports and school records. However, even in the absence of legal change, the right to identity includes having one’s chosen name and pronouns respected.
committee: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity
committees: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity

text: In many contexts, educators, school staff or peers may refuse to use, or be legally prohibited from using, a transgender or gender-diverse student’s preferred name or pronouns, which can cause significant psychological harm, lead to forced outing and contribute to the erasure of the student’s identity.66 Educators may instead insist on the use of an individual’s legal name and pronouns only. In some cases, parents must provide approval for schools to use the chosen pronouns of their child. 67 There are jurisdictions where students have been suspended or expelled for using their chosen names or pronouns.68 The lack of clear policies, guidance and training on these 60 Submissions by Commissioner for Human Rights of Poland, Human Rights Watch, RSFL Ungdom, Santa Marta Centre, Save the Children Youth Sweden, Single Step Foundation, SOS Homophobie, Vidhi Centre for Legal Policy and Young Pride Foundation, and joint submission by Rainbow Action and DDing Dong. 61 Submission by Commission on Human Rights of the Philippines. 62 Submission by Outright International. 63 Submission by LESLAC Network. 64 Submission by Egale. 65 Submissions by Single Step Foundation and Youth Pride. 66 Submissions by Canadian Human Rights Commission, Save the Children Youth Sweden and others. 67 Submissions by Egale and SOS Homophobie. 68 Submissions by Coming Out, joint report by Certified NPO ReBit, Tnet, Proud Futures and General Incorporated Association Niji-zu, and others. 12/21 matters often leaves educators unprepared, resulting in inconsistent practices that depend on individual awareness and goodwill.69
committee: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity
committees: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity

text: Educational institutions may require that enrolment forms, examination materials, diplomas, graduation records, transcripts and other official documents reflect a student’s legal name and gender marker.70 When these do not align with a student’s gender identity, they create significant barriers to accessing higher education, employment and other opportunities. The mismatch between official educational records and a student’s gender identity can result in discrimination, exclusion and undue scrutiny. As a positive example, the University of Sarajevo allows students to specify the gender they wish to have reflected on their diploma, offering a more inclusive and respectful approach to documentation.71
committee: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity
committees: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity

text: Several States and local authorities have adopted good practices to support transgender and gender-diverse students. In Scotland, education guidance requires teachers to use students’ chosen names and pronouns, with informal and formal name change options.72 In Cuba, educators may use preferred names without restriction. 73 Some local councils in the United Kingdom have developed support guidelines, though some were later withdrawn following opposition. 74 In Brazil, students are guaranteed the right to use uniforms, facilities and names aligned with their gender identity. 75 Spanish law affirms gender self-determination in schools, mandates inclusive curricula, bans conversion therapy and ensures access to aligned facilities and counselling.76 In India, transgender students may use public toilets that match their self-identified gender and courts have upheld their right to participate in gendered activities accordingly.77 E. Lack of access to affirming healthcare and mental health services
committee: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity
committees: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity

text: Health and well-being are fundamental to the achievement of educational outcomes and permeate all aspects of school life. Basic school health services should promote and protect physical and mental health, foster life skills, support cognitive and socioemotional development and encourage healthy lifestyles in a safe and inclusive learning environment. 78 However, many schools and universities lack adequate physical and mental health services, and where such services exist, they are often not inclusive or affirming of LGBT learners.79 In some cases, these services may actively discriminate against LGBT students or exacerbate their distress, particularly with regard to mental and emotional health. Fear of discrimination discourages many LGBT students from seeking support. 80 With some exceptions, most Governments have not developed appropriate training, protocols or guidance for school psychologists, counsellors and other mental health professionals. As a result, school-based professionals often lack the necessary knowledge and awareness to 69 Submissions by Roberto Kulpa and Adrianna Zabrzewska and Saplinq. 70 Submission by Háttér Society, Single Step Foundation and others. 71 Submission by Sarajevo Open Centre. 72 Submission by Just like Us. 73 Submission by ILGA World. 74 Submission by Just Like Us. 75 Submission by Government of Brazil. 76 Submission by Zaira García Dafonte (Sorginlore Social Association). 77 Submission by Vidhi Centre for Legal Policy. 78 World Health Organization and UNESCO, Making Every School a Health-promoting School: Global Standards and Indicators, 2021. 79 Submission by Association Legebitra, Bundesverband Trans, Government of Brazil and others. 80 Submission by La Asociación Ciudadana ACCEDER. address the specific health needs of LGBT learners, and may in some cases respond in openly discriminatory or harmful ways.
committee: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity
committees: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity

text: In all regions, LGBT students may face pressure from school staff or mental health professionals to change their sexual orientation or gender identity, including through so-called “conversion therapy”.81 Instead of supporting self-discovery, some authority figures convey that LGBT students are ill or that their behaviour is immoral or wrong – messages intended to induce shame and conformity. In some cases, school professionals have recommended or mandated “rehabilitative counselling”, abstinence or heterosexual relationships as a “cure”.82 Few States provide adequate protection against such harmful practices, leaving LGBT students, especially children, vulnerable to coercion by trusted adults.83 F. Consequences of violence, bullying and exclusion
committee: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity
committees: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity

text: Bullying, harassment and discriminatory environments often prevent LGBT students from fully participating in the extracurricular life of schools and universities, including events, clubs, sports and other activities.84 In some cases, students have been denied the right to establish LGBT student groups, or have refrained from doing so due to hostile educational climates.85 Existing clubs have been forced to disband in response to increasing social and political pressure. LGBT-related events are sometimes banned and peaceful activities such as pride walks or film screenings have been met with police intervention or other forms of violence.86 As a positive example, legislation in Spain promotes the development of safe spaces within schools, including support groups for transgender youth, as part of a broader commitment to inclusive education.87 The Romanian Equality Body has recognized discrimination in several important cases, such as when students were denied the right to form an LGBT student group, or when teachers made derogatory comments, although these decisions have had limited policy impact.88
committee: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity
committees: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity

text: The physical and psychosocial harm experienced by LGBT students – especially when subjected to bullying or forced gender conformity – can disrupt their education. 89 Confronted with the choice between safety and schooling, many disengage to protect their well-being, which may take the form of changing schools, skipping classes or dropping out – often at higher rates than non-LGBT peers. Transgender and gender-diverse youth are particularly at risk.90 These patterns lead to lower academic achievement and long-term exclusion from economic and social 81 Conversion therapy is an umbrella term to describe interventions premised on the belief that a person’s sexual orientation and gender identity, including gender expression, can and should be changed or suppressed when they do not fall under what other actors in a given setting and time perceive as the desirable norm, in particular when the person is lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender or gender diverse (see A/HRC/44/53). 82 Submissions by ILGA World, LESLAC Network, Outright International and others. 83 A/HRC/44/53. Submissions by La Asociación Ciudadana ACCEDER and Commission on Human Rights of the Philippines. 84 Submissions by Bundesverband Trans and others. 85 Submissions by ASEAN SOGIE Caucus, Kaos GL, Maria Ecaterina Nistor, Saplinq, joint submission by UniKuir and the Advocates for Human Rights, and others. 86 Submission by Kaos GL and joint submission by UniKuir and the Advocates for Human Rights. 87 Submission by Zaira García Dafonte (Sorginlore Social Association). 88 Submission by Maria Ecaterina Nistor. 89 Submissions by La Asociación Ciudadana ACCEDER, Canadian Human Rights Commission, Save the Children Youth Sweden and others. 90 Submissions by Canadian Human Rights Commission and others. 14/21 opportunities. The cumulative effects, including poor mental health and school withdrawal, heighten the risk of poverty, homelessness and isolation.
committee: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity
committees: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity

text: Discrimination, bullying, forced gender conformity, social exclusion and the lack of supportive educators and mental health services, as well as ineffective complaint mechanisms, deeply affect LGBT learners’ mental health, academic outcomes and overall well-being. Many report feeling isolated, despondent and hopeless. Persistent fear, anxiety and depression impair motivation, concentration and engagement, leading to withdrawal from academic, extracurricular and social life. Surveys from all regions show high rates of suicidal ideation, self-harm and suicide attempts among LGBT youth – especially transgender students.91 The fact that LGBT-focused suicide prevention hotlines report spikes in calls during debates on anti-LGBT legislation is evidence of the mental health impact of hostile political climates.92 G. Protective factors: teachers and involvement of civil society organizations
committee: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity
committees: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity

text: Surveys have found that LGBT individuals who attend supportive schools are significantly more likely to report optimism about their future. Educators, counsellors and other school staff can play a profoundly protective role in the lives of LGBT students. When these adults are affirming and proactive, LGBT learners are more likely to feel safe, attend school regularly and experience improved mental health and academic outcomes.93 Supportive staff can themselves become targets of discrimination, however. Educators who identify as LGBT – or who advocate for the rights and inclusion of LGBT students – may face harassment, unfounded disciplinary action and even dismissal by school or university authorities.94 Such reprisals contribute to a broader climate of fear and silence and discourage other educators from engaging with these issues. As a result, many teachers avoid addressing LGBT topics altogether, out of concern about negative reactions from parents, communities or administrators, which leads to self-censorship and the absence of inclusive and affirming discussions about diversity in the classroom.95
committee: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity
committees: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity

text: In the absence of LGBT teachers, professors or other school staff, all learners are deprived of the opportunity to engage with diverse role models. Visible representation of LGBT adults in educational settings helps to normalize diverse identities, reduce prejudice and counter internalized stigma. For LGBT students in particular, LGBT educators often serve as trusted adults with whom they can confide and find affirmation. When students do not see themselves reflected in any adult role models, they may feel less hopeful about their futures and more disconnected from their school or university community. In Argentina, teachers’ organizations have voiced concern over the Government’s decision to eliminate content on sexual orientation and gender identity from the curriculum and have emphasized its detrimental impact on the rights and well-being of LGBT students.96
committee: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity
committees: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity

text: Civil society organizations play an important and constructive role in supporting educational institutions to create inclusive and affirming environments for LGBT learners. They offer expert guidance and training for educators, staff and students on 91 Submissions by Canadian Human Rights Commission, Commission on Human Rights of the Philippines, HRAU Timor-Leste, joint report by Certified NPO ReBit, Tnet, Proud Futures and General Incorporated Association Niji-zu, and others. 92 UNESCO, “LGBTIQ+ youth: bullying and violence at school”. 93 Ibid. 94 Submissions by Coming Out, Kaos GL, Háttér Society and others. 95 Submissions by ILGA World and Bundesverband Trans. 96 Submission by ILGA World. issues of non-discrimination, inclusion and comprehensive sexuality education. The submissions received provide a number of positive examples of schools, colleges and universities cooperating with civil society organizations in all regions. 97 Such organizations also frequently provide services such as helplines, support groups and counselling, to which schools can refer LGBT students for additional support. 98
committee: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity
committees: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity

text: In many contexts, cooperation between educational institutions and civil society organizations is either absent or limited to ad hoc initiatives by individual schools, rather than being supported by clear governmental policy or institutional mandates. 99 In several States, legal restrictions on freedom of expression and association for LGBT persons hinder the formation or operation of LGBT organizations. Even where such organizations do exist, they may be prohibited from engaging with schools or face opposition from parents, communities or authorities when they do.100 In some countries where collaboration had previously occurred, increasingly hostile social and legal environments have led to the curtailment or termination of these partnerships and undermined efforts to create inclusive and supportive educational spaces.101 IV. Restrictions on access to information about sexual orientation, gender identity and sexuality
committee: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity
committees: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity

text: Evidence-based guidance from UNESCO, the World Health Organization and numerous professional associations of doctors, psychologists, educators and parents consistently affirms that it is safe and appropriate to teach children and young people about gender equality and about diverse sexual orientations, gender identities and expressions, in an age-appropriate manner.102 Research shows that comprehensive sexuality education, defined as a curriculum-based approach to teaching and learning about the cognitive, emotional, physical and social dimensions of sexuality, not only supports healthy development but also contributes to reducing sexual harassment, gender-based violence and intimate partner violence.103
committee: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity
committees: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity

text: In educational settings, information about LGBT topics should be integrated into relevant areas of the curriculum, including social studies, history, citizenship, literature and health. The inclusion of diverse identities in everyday lessons affirms that LGBT persons are an integral part of society, rather than an exception. 104 Comprehensive sexuality education should be inclusive of all individuals. It should promote human rights, healthy relationships, gender equality, well-being, empathy, respect, personal autonomy and informed consent.105
committee: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity
committees: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity

text: In many States, standard curricula and textbooks either omit topics related to LGBT individuals, sexual orientation, gender identity, tolerance and diversity, or portray 97 Submissions by ASEAN SOGIE Caucus, Pyali Chatterjee and others, Government of Slovenia, Jo Brassington and Sue Sanders, Association Legebitra, Roberto Kulpa and Adrianna Zabrzewska, SOS Homophobie and Qun Jelesi. 98 Submissions by Step by Step and Government of Slovenia. 99 Submissions by Angaza Foundation, Bundesverband Trans, HRAU Timor-Leste, ILGA World and Maria Ecaterina Nistor. 100 Submissions by Angaza Foundation, ASEAN SOGIE Caucus and Qun Jelesi. 101 Submissions by ASEAN SOGIE Caucus, ILGA World and Step by Step. 102 UNESCO, Out in the Open: Education Sector Responses to Violence Based on Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity/Expression, 2016. 103 UNESCO, “Q&A: ending school violence for better mental health and learning”, 2023. 104 Recommendation CM/Rec(2010)5 of the Committee of Ministers of the Council of Europe to member states on measures to combat discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. See also European Union Agency for Fundamental Rights, Professionally Speaking: Challenges to Achieving Equality for LGBT People, 2016. 105 OHCHR, “A compendium on comprehensive sexuality education” (2023). 16/21 LGBT persons in discriminatory, demeaning or pejorative ways. 106 Comprehensive sexuality education is absent in numerous contexts; where it does exist, it often excludes topics related to sexual orientation and gender identity, or is implemented inconsistently.107 In some cases, curricula or classroom instruction materials actively reinforce discriminatory attitudes and harmful stereotypes, thereby contributing to hostile and unsafe learning environments.108 “Moral education” or religious instruction may promote the idea that homosexuality or diverse gender identities are deviant and should be corrected or eliminated. LGBT individuals may be presented as a threat to “traditional values”.109 Furthermore, in many States, sexuality education, under labels such as “family life education”, focuses narrowly on reproduction, binary gender roles and the heteronormative nuclear family model.110 In some instances, sexuality education and teacher training are outsourced to religious actors who promote discriminatory views against LGBT persons.111
committee: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity
committees: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity

text: There are notable good practices concerning the inclusion of sexual orientation and gender identity in sexuality education and mainstream curricula. In Cyprus, sexuality education is compulsory and includes topics such as homophobia and gender identity, although implementation remains inconsistent. 112 In Spain, both sexuality education and general education programmes are required to include content on gender and sexual diversity, grounded in human rights and non-discrimination principles. This content is mandated at all stages of education and is designed to challenge binary stereotypes and pathologizing narratives.113 The national curriculum in Sweden integrates sexual orientation and gender identity across multiple subjects and includes comprehensive teacher training in sexuality education. Similar efforts have been introduced in different parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina.114 In Scotland, the Government has adopted a national approach to LGBT-inclusive education, which requires age-appropriate, LGBT-inclusive content to be taught across curriculum areas and education levels. An LGBT group has been engaged by the Scottish Government to implement mandatory training for all teachers in this methodology. 115
committee: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity
committees: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity

text: There are deeply concerning global trends in which State, regional and local authorities – as well as education officials, cultural and religious leaders, and parents – have sought to restrict or censor information related to sexual orientation and gender identity at all levels of education, including in higher education. 116 These efforts have included the proposal and adoption of laws, policies and administrative practices aimed at removing such topics from curricula, including from comprehensive sexuality education, or prohibiting any discussion of sexual 106 Submissions by National Human Rights Commission of Korea and Kaos GL. 107 Submissions by Comisión de Derechos Humanos de la Ciudad de México, Defensoría del Pueblo de Ecuador, ECOM, Government of Cyprus, Government of Guatemala, Government of the Republic of South Africa, Government of Ecuador, Government of Switzerland, Save the Children Thailand and others. 108 Submission by Roberto Kulpa and Adrianna Zabrzewska. 109 Submissions by ASEAN SOGIE Caucus, Coming Out, Saplinq and others. 110 Submissions by Háttér Society and others. 111 Submissions by LESLAC and Akahatá – Equipo de Trabajo en Sexualidad y Géneros, Asociación Civil. 112 Submission by Government of Cyprus. 113 Submission by Zaira García Dafonte (Sorginlore Social Association). 114 Submissions by Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, RFSL Ungdom and Sarajevo Open Centre. 115 Submission by Time for Inclusive Education. 116 Submissions by Commission consultative des droits de l’homme (Luxembourg), Comisión de Derechos Humanos de la Ciudad de México, Human Rights Watch, ILGA World, Outright International, Santa Marta Centre, Saplinq, UniKuir and Advocates for Human Rights, Qun Jelesi and others, and joint report by Certified NPO ReBit, Tnet, Proud Futures and General Incorporated Association Niji-zu. orientation and gender identity within school settings.117 Often, these measures are justified through unfounded claims that addressing these topics constitutes “indoctrination”, promotes so-called “gender ideology” or conflicts with religious values.118 In several States, recent initiatives to introduce inclusive curricula have failed in the face of hostile and discriminatory political rhetoric.119 Schools that have attempted to foster positive and inclusive environments for LGBT students have, in some instances, been subjected to targeted scrutiny, hostile inspections and other forms of institutional retaliation.120
committee: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity
committees: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity

text: Parental opposition also plays a role in efforts to suppress access to LGBTinclusive content in education.121 In some States, laws allow parents to withdraw their children from specific lessons, or require parents to opt in, including those related to sexuality education and LGBT topics.122 Even in jurisdictions where such content is compulsory and there is no provision for parental opt-out, there have been concerted efforts – often led or supported by parents – to challenge or protest LGBT-inclusive curricula and to demand exemptions. In certain cases, these attempts have been reviewed and ultimately rejected by courts, affirming the importance of inclusive education grounded in human rights principles.123
committee: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity
committees: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity

text: In contexts where sexual orientation and gender identity are included in, or not explicitly excluded from, curricula – including in comprehensive sexuality education – teachers frequently lack the training, resources and institutional support necessary to address these topics effectively and from a human rights-based perspective.124 As a result, educators often rely on personal judgment, interest or independent research to incorporate LGBT-related content.125 In some cases, teachers who attempt to do so face intense opposition, harassment or even legal threats, leading many to self-censor.126 Educators and schools have been subjected to criticism and punitive measures for addressing sexual orientation and gender identity in the classroom and have been compelled to remove symbols of support, such as rainbow flags or posters indicating “Safe Spaces” for LGBT students.127
committee: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity
committees: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity

text: When learners turn to alternative sources for information about sexual orientation and gender identity, their access to accurate, honest and science-based content is often further restricted. In some States, school and public libraries have been compelled to remove books and periodicals containing LGBT-related information, even in jurisdictions with strong national anti-discrimination protections – often due to pressure from parents or community groups. 128 Online 117 See A/HRC/56/49, para. 38. See also submissions by Akahatá – Equipo de Trabajo en Sexualidad y Géneros, Asociación Civil, Coming Out, Egale, LESLAC Network, ILGALAC National Front of LGBTIQ+ Organizations Pride and Struggle, Outright International, Sarajevo Open Centre and others. 118 See A/HRC/56/49, para. 38. See also submissions by Human Rights Watch, Outright International, LESLAC Network. 119 Submissions by Government of Brazil, LESLAC Network and Outright International. 120 Submission by Roberto Kulpa and Adrianna Zabrzewska and others. 121 Submission by Save the Children Youth Sweden and others. 122 Submission by Maria Ecaterina Nistor, Just Like Us and others. 123 Submissions by Comisión de Derechos Humanos de la Ciudad de México, Just Like Us, Saplinq and Time for Inclusive Education. 124 Submission by Save the Children Thailand, SOS Homophobie, Vidhi Centre for Legal Policy and others. 125 Submission by Association Legebitra. 126 Submission by Comisión de Derechos Humanos de la Ciudad de México and others. 127 Submissions by Human Rights Watch and Report Out. 128 Submission by Akahatá – Equipo de Trabajo en Sexualidad y Géneros, Asociación Civil, ASEAN SOGIE Caucus, Jo Brassington and Sue Sanders, Legebrita, RFSL Ungdom and others, and joint submission by Rainbow Action and DDing Dong. 18/21 sources, while more widely available, vary significantly in accuracy and reliability. 129 In certain countries, access to information on gender identity and sexual orientation, whether through literature, online content or peer support groups, is criminalized, and individuals who publish or seek such information may face legal penalties. 130 These restrictions contribute to the erasure of diverse student identities, undermine efforts to promote understanding and tolerance and deny all learners the opportunity to learn more about themselves and others.
committee: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity
committees: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity

text: The submissions for the present report indicate that, overwhelmingly, Governments do not collect relevant data related to LGBT learners, although some Governments collect some data related to LGBT individuals more generally. Civil society organizations and some national human rights institutions do collect data at the national and subnational levels on the experience of LGBT youth in education, although those data are limited. The absence of data conceals the scale and nature of the challenges faced by sexual orientation and gender identity-diverse students and hinders informed policymaking and targeted interventions. V. Conclusions
committee: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity
committees: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity

text: The human right to education is fundamental to individual dignity, selfdetermination and development. Yet, for many LGBT learners, this right remains elusive due to widespread and persistent violence, discrimination and exclusion in educational settings. Bullying, whether physical, psychological or sexual, is a pervasive reality for LGBT students in all regions of the world. Often tolerated or ignored by school authorities, such abuse not only violates learners’ rights to safety and dignity, but also drives absenteeism, academic disengagement, early school leaving and severe mental health consequences, including elevated risks of self-harm and suicide.
committee: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity
committees: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity

text: These harms are exacerbated when school systems fail to provide effective protection, affirming support services or inclusive curricula. The lack of legal recognition of gender identity, the enforcement of binary norms and punitive disciplinary measures further entrench marginalization.
committee: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity
committees: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity

text: Nonetheless, promising practices offer pathways to change. States that have adopted inclusive anti-discrimination laws, mandated LGBT-inclusive curricula, established safe and confidential reporting mechanisms and invested in teacher training and mental health support offer important models for fostering safe and inclusive learning environments. Collaboration with civil society organizations and the visible presence of LGBT educators also play a crucial role in cultivating respect, empathy and belonging in schools.
committee: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity
committees: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity

text: The full realization of the right to education for LGBT persons requires that States implement concrete measures to dismantle structural barriers, address the root causes of exclusion and create environments where all learners can thrive in safety, equality and dignity. VI. Recommendations
committee: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity
committees: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity

text: With regard to addressing the broader environment in which discrimination and violence occur and promoting equality and 129 Submission by ECOM. 130 Submission by Coming Out. non-discrimination for LGBT learners at all levels and in all types of educational institutions, States should: (a) Decriminalize consensual same-sex conduct in accordance with international human rights standards; (b) Eliminate legal and administrative restrictions on the rights to freedom of expression, peaceful assembly and association, including those based on sexual orientation and gender identity; (c) Adopt and implement comprehensive anti-discrimination legislation that explicitly includes sexual orientation and gender identity as protected grounds; (d) Ensure that school anti-bullying, anti-harassment and child protection policies explicitly include protections for LGBT learners; (e) Prohibit practices such as expulsion, denial of admission or disciplinary action based on sexual orientation or gender identity; (f) Take concrete measures to combat and eliminate all forms of social stigmatization, discrimination and violence based on sexual orientation and gender identity; (g) Take appropriate legislative, administrative, educational and other measures to prevent and eliminate harmful practices aimed at changing or suppressing a person’s sexual orientation or gender identity, including so-called “conversion therapies” and punitive responses to non-normative gender expression; (h) Promote public awareness and understanding of sexual and gender diversity, including through campaigns targeting parents, families and communities, and address the harmful impact of disinformation and discriminatory rhetoric; (i) Ensure the meaningful participation of LGBT persons and organizations in the development, implementation and evaluation of laws, policies and programmes that affect them, in accordance with the principles of transparency, inclusivity and non-discrimination.
committee: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity
committees: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity

text: With regard to addressing violence and bullying, States, educational institutions and other stakeholders should: (a) Establish and enforce a zero-tolerance policy for all forms of violence and bullying in educational settings, including cyberbullying, with explicit inclusion of protections for LGBT learners; (b) Take proactive measures to prevent and respond to bullying of all students, including targeted actions to address the specific risks faced by LGBT learners; (c) Establish safe, accessible, confidential and effective mechanisms for students to report bullying, harassment and discrimination; (d) Develop and apply fair, transparent and effective remedies and disciplinary procedures to address incidents of violence and bullying; (e) Provide clear protocols and regular training for teachers, administrators and school staff to recognize, prevent and respond to incidents of discrimination or violence, and to offer appropriate support to affected students; 20/21 (f) Implement comprehensive systems for monitoring and evaluating violence in and around educational institutions, including disaggregated data collection; (g) In consultation with LGBT organizations, design and implement methods and protocols for the collection and use of data on the experiences of LGBT learners, in order to inform evidence-based public policies and promote accountability.
committee: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity
committees: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity

text: With regard to gender identity recognition, States should: (a) Adopt legislation that enables transgender and gender-diverse persons to change their legal name and gender marker through a procedure based on self-determination. Such a process should be simple, administrative in nature, free from abusive requirements and, in the case of children, accessible in a manner that takes into account their evolving capacities and views, consistent with the best interests of the child; (b) Permit the use of chosen names and pronouns in educational settings, including on school records and official documentation, irrespective of whether legal gender recognition has been obtained; (c) Ensure safe and non-discriminatory access to school facilities, including bathrooms and changing rooms, in accordance with students’ selfidentified gender; (d) Eliminate gendered requirements in school uniforms, dress codes and appearance standards so as to allow students to express their gender identity freely and without penalty; (e) Establish and uphold confidentiality protections for LGBT students, particularly minors, including with respect to the disclosure of sexual orientation or gender identity in accordance with the student’s consent and best interests.
committee: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity
committees: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity

text: With regard to creating safe and inclusive school environments, educational institutions should: (a) Establish gender-inclusive facilities, including gender-neutral bathrooms and changing rooms, to ensure the safety, dignity and comfort of all students; (b) Display visible affirmations of diversity and inclusion, such as inclusive signage, posters and symbols that reflect the presence and human rights of LGBT persons; (c) Support and facilitate the formation and operation of student-led LGBT groups and other affinity organizations that promote inclusion, peer support and awareness; (d) Ensure that classrooms and school or community libraries include a diverse range of age-appropriate books, periodicals and learning materials that reflect sexual and gender diversity, promote understanding and counteract stereotypes and prejudice.
committee: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity
committees: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity

text: With regard to comprehensive sexuality education and inclusive curricula, States should: (a) Implement age-appropriate, evidence-based and scientifically accurate comprehensive sexuality education that affirms human rights and is inclusive of concepts related to sexual orientation, gender identity and expression, and diverse family structures; (b) Promote diversity and inclusion across the education system by ensuring that curricula, subjects and educational materials reflect a broad range of human experiences and identities, including those related to sexual orientation and gender identity, in a manner that fosters understanding, respect and equality; (c) Develop and implement mandatory, ongoing training programmes for teachers, school administrators and educational personnel on inclusive pedagogical approaches that promote diversity, equality and non-discrimination, including in relation to sexual orientation and gender identity; (d) Collaborate with LGBT organizations and experts in the development, implementation and evaluation of inclusive educational content and teacher training initiatives.
committee: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity
committees: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity

text: With regard to mental health and support services, educational institutions should: (a) Ensure the presence of trained and qualified mental health professionals and support staff who provide services that are inclusive, affirming and responsive to the specific needs of LGBT learners; (b) Guarantee access to safe, confidential, child-sensitive and traumainformed counselling and psychosocial support within the educational environment; (c) Provide accessible information, resources and quality referral pathways for LGBT learners experiencing mental health crises or psychosocial distress; (d) Establish coordination mechanisms to connect LGBT learners with competent and affirming community-based health and support services; (e) Develop and implement programmes to assist students who face or are at risk of family rejection, including access to counselling, shelter and other protective measures.
committee: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity
committees: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity

text: With regard to community outreach and education, States should: (a) Promote dialogue and awareness among parents, caregivers and families to foster understanding, acceptance and inclusion of LGBT persons, including in educational settings; (b) Establish and strengthen partnerships with local civil society organizations, including LGBT-led groups, as well as community leaders and stakeholders, to support inclusive education and combat discrimination; (c) Design and implement outreach and education strategies that are culturally appropriate and responsive to the needs of rural, Indigenous and minority communities, taking into account intersecting forms of discrimination and vulnerability.

text: The mandate of the Independent Expert on protection against violence and discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity was established by the Human Rights Council in 2016 in its resolution 32/2.1 Vitit Muntarbhorn, an emeritus law professor from Thailand, was appointed to the post, as the first mandate holder. He began his mandate in November 2016. The Independent Expert is mandated to report annually to the Human Rights Council and the General Assembly. The present report is the first by the Independent Expert under a three-year mandate and it covers the first few months of his work, up until March 2017. The Independent Expert wishes to warmly thank Governments, international organizations, non-governmental organizations, communities, individuals and other stakeholders for their kind support. He welcomes the information sent by numerous contributors, which will progressively be integrated into his analysis and reports.
committee: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity
committees: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity

text: Everyone has some form of sexual orientation and of gender identity. 2 Sexual orientation has an external dimension — it indicates a person’s sexual inclination and feelings towards others. Gender identity has an internal dimension — the term refers to how a person self-identifies in regard to his or her own gender, which may be different from the gender assigned at birth. Even though human rights are inherent to everyone and involve protection for all persons without exception, regrettably persons with an actual or perceived sexual orientation and/or gender identity diverging from a particular societal concept are at times targeted for violence and discrimination, and violations are pervasive in numerous settings. Killings, rapes, mutilations, torture, cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment, arbitrary detentions, abductions, harassment, physical and mental assaults, bullying suffered from a young age, pressures leading to suicide, and discriminatory gestures and measures — aggravated by incitement to hatred — in relation to sexual orientation and gender identity, are widespread on several fronts. These negative incidents call for effective action to counter the violence and discrimination in their various forms. This is a local-global phenomenon that traverses the home, the educational system, community relations, national scenarios and the international setting.
committee: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity
committees: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity

text: The present report is thus anchored on the belief that while the diversity among human beings on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity should be recognized (i.e. diversity in humanity), it is essential to harness and reinforce, from a young age, mutual respect, tolerance and understanding, compliance with human rights, and a sense of humanity and inclusivity inherent in that diversity (i.e. humanity in diversity), under the umbrella of international human rights law, to accord protection for all and to all. II. Methodology

committees: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity

text: The work of the Independent Expert follows the mandate set by the Human Rights Council as part of the Council’s special procedures. From the outset, the Independent Expert has adopted an approach of open and constructive dialogue and of engagement with 1 See A/HRC/29/23 for background information. 2 For some definitions, see Living Free and Equal: What States Are Doing to Tackle Violence and Discrimination against Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Transgender and Intersex People (United Nations publication, 2016), pp. 18 and 19, available from www.ohchr.org/Documents/Publications/LivingFreeAndEqual.pdf: “Gender identity reflects a deeply felt and experienced sense of one’s own gender … Transgender (sometimes shortened to “trans”) is an umbrella term used to describe people with a wide range of identities … Trans women identify as women but were classified as males when they were born. Trans men identify as men but were classified female when they were born … Intersex people are born with physical or biological sex characteristics including sexual anatomy … that do not fit the typical definitions of male or female … Sexual orientation refers to a person’s physical, romantic and/or emotional attraction towards other people … Gay men and lesbian women are attracted to individuals of the same sex as themselves. Heterosexual people are attracted to individuals of a different sex from themselves. Bisexual ... people may be attracted to individuals of the same or different sex.” a broad range of stakeholders. Shortly after assuming the mandate, the Independent Expert held a public consultation on the mandate to engage in dialogue with Governments, nongovernmental organizations, international organizations and other actors, in Geneva, in January 2017. The aim was to consult broadly on the work under the mandate. The consultation was webcast publicly so as to enable global access to it. The various key issues raised during the consultation are reflected in the present report. Since the beginning of his work on the mandate, he has gathered a wide range of information — some written, some oral — to help prepare the present report. This is an introductory report — a window through which to gauge his approach — and it provides an overview of issues to be explored in more detail in subsequent reports. It is the Independent Expert’s intention to balance and cross-check between a variety of sources of information — governmental, intergovernmental and non-governmental. He does this with a view to ensuring objectivity of analysis in his capacity as Independent Expert; the present report was written and typed by the Independent Expert himself.

text: Other aspects of the methodology include plans for country visits, action to respond to communications to address negative situations pertaining to sexual orientation and gender identity, and cooperation with a broad range of actors, including affected groups and individuals, Governments, regional and national human rights institutions, other special procedure mandate holders, human rights treaty bodies and United Nations agencies. The first country visit carried out by the mandate holder was to Argentina, in March 2017. His end-of-mission statement is available online.3 A separate report on his mission to Argentina will be issued subsequently. The Independent Expert warmly thanks the Government and people of Argentina for their excellent cooperation. He was impressed with many key developments in the country, which provide positive lessons for the rest of the world community, while also bearing in mind a range of challenges. III. Mandate

text: There are various essentials that should be taken into account in undertaking work related to this mandate. Firstly, words are very sensitive under the mandate. From his very first days undertaking his tasks, the Independent Expert has been struck by the quest for balanced terminology concerning sexual orientation and gender identity. The acronym “LGBT” appears in discussions and is closely linked with this mandate. 4 It stands for lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender (persons). Many people are confused by the terms “transgender man/trans man” and “transgender woman/trans woman”. The former denotes those classified biologically at birth as women, who wish to have their self-identity recognized as men, while the latter means the converse: those classified biologically at birth as men, who wish to have their self-identity recognized as women. The term “intersex” (person) — the “I” in “LGBTI” — even when explained as referring to persons with atypical sex characteristics, is not easily understood.5 The mandate will cover this group where there is a link with sexual orientation and gender identity, while recognizing that the group has special features not necessarily related to sexual orientation and gender identity.
committee: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity
committees: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity

text: Secondly, regrettably, every society has many pejorative terms used to designate various groups and persons as regards their sexual orientation or gender identity. Semantic negativities add to a lack of (or difficulties in) understanding and to misconceptions — fuelling narrow mindsets — about those who fall under the rubric of sexual orientation and gender identity, and this dilemma contributes to the ensuing violence and discrimination. There is thus an invitation to clarify the terms used and to avoid negative terminology, to help prevent misunderstandings and to stem biases and prejudices which breed various “phobias” and which are found, to a lesser or greater extent, in all societies. Many United 3 See www.ohchr.org/EN/NewsEvents/Pages/DisplayNews.aspx?NewsID=21343&LangID=E. 4 Ibid. 5 Ibid. Nations programmes, underlining the plight of persons, now employ the denomination “LGBT”, and add an “I” when referring to intersex persons (thus “LGBTI”).6

text: Thirdly, the preamble to Human Rights Council resolution 32/2, which established the mandate of the Independent Expert, is a key reminder that there are historical, cultural, socioeconomic, political and religious sensitivities, and that there is a need to respond to them in a measured and judicious way, bearing in mind their connectivity with international human rights standards. The preamble reaffirms the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. The relationship between international human rights law — particularly its universality and indivisibility — and national and regional particularities is then evoked in a famous passage from the Vienna Declaration and Programme of Action, adopted at the World Conference on Human Rights held in Vienna in1993, which is cited in Council resolution 32/2 as follows: Recalling that the Vienna Declaration and Programme of Action affirms that all human rights are universal, indivisible and interdependent and interrelated, that the international community must treat human rights globally in a fair and equal manner, on the same footing, and with the same emphasis, and that while the significance of national and regional particularities and various historical, cultural and religious backgrounds must be borne in mind, it is the duty of States, regardless of their political, economic and cultural systems, to promote and protect all human rights and fundamental freedoms.

committees: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity

text: Fourthly, the preamble also emphasizes the need to maintain joint ownership of the international human rights agenda and to strengthen action against racism, racial discrimination, xenophobia and related intolerance in all their forms — all of which may be interrelated with violence and discrimination in regard to sexual orientation and gender identity. 7 This introduces the intersectionality between sexual orientation and gender identity on the one hand, and other issues, such as race and others forms of discrimination.

committees: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity

text: Fifthly, the Independent Expert is requested under Council resolution 32/2, as follows: “ (a) To assess the implementation of existing international human rights instruments with regard to ways to overcome violence and discrimination against persons on the basis of their sexual orientation or gender identity, while identifying both best practices and gaps; (b) To raise awareness of violence and discrimination against persons on the basis of their sexual orientation or gender identity, and to identify and address the root causes of violence and discrimination; (c) To engage in dialogue and to consult with States and other relevant stakeholders, including United Nations agencies, programmes and funds, regional human rights mechanisms, national human rights institutions, regional mechanisms, civil society organizations and academic institutions; (d) To work in cooperation with States in order to foster the implementation of measures that contribute to the protection of all persons against violence and discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity; (e) To address the multiple, intersecting and aggravated forms of violence and discrimination faced by persons on the basis of their sexual orientation and gender identity; (f) To conduct, facilitate and support the provision of advisory services, technical assistance, capacity-building and international cooperation in support of 6 See, for example, the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) paper issued on 25 November 2015 entitled “The role of the United Nations in combating discrimination and violence against individuals based on sexual orientation and gender identity”. 7 See Human Rights Council resolution 32/2. national efforts to combat violence and discrimination against persons on the basis of their sexual orientation or gender identity.”8

text: Key elements emanating from the mandate cited above can be summarized into five main areas, as follows: (a) implementation of international instruments, with the identification of good practices and gaps; (b) awareness of the violence and discrimination issue, and linkage with root causes; (c) engagement, consultation and cooperation with States and other stakeholders; (d) addressing multiple, intersecting and aggravated forms of violence and discrimination; and (e) support for international cooperation and related services to assist national efforts. These elements will be responded to in greater detail below, after a brief situational analysis of violence and discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity.

text: In keeping with the role of the special procedures, the work of the Independent Expert is related to at least four functions: (a) preparing reports on the mandate; (b) periodically carrying out country visits to learn about local situations and sharing those lessons with the international community; (c) receiving communications/complaints regarding human rights violations, from victims, and acting on them through contact and leverage with the State or entity concerned; and (d) cooperating with other actors. All these functions are now operational. Importantly, communications are being received and acted upon, for example in regard to threats to human rights defenders working on sexual orientation and gender identity issues. IV. Panorama

text: According to the statement from 12 United Nations entities on ending violence and discrimination against lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender and intersex people: The United Nations and others have documented widespread physical and psychological violence against LGBTI persons in all regions — including murder, assault, kidnapping, rape, sexual violence, as well as torture and ill-treatment in institutional and other settings. LGBTI youth and lesbian, bisexual and transgender women are at particular risk of physical, psychological and sexual violence in family and community settings. LGBTI persons often face violence and discrimination when seeking refuge from persecution and in humanitarian emergencies. They may also face abuse in medical settings, including unethical and harmful so-called “therapies” to change sexual orientation, forced or coercive sterilization, forced genital and anal examinations, and unnecessary surgery and treatment on intersex children without their consent. In many countries, the response to these violations is inadequate, they are underreported and often not properly investigated and prosecuted, leading to widespread impunity, and lack of justice, remedies and support for victims. Human rights defenders combating these violations are frequently persecuted and face discriminatory restrictions on their activities.9

text: The following gaps and challenges are outlined in Living Free and Equal: Criminalization, discriminatory attitudes, harassment by police, stigma, ill-treatment in detention and medical settings, lack of protective legislation, absence of complaints mechanisms, lack of trust in law enforcement officials and of awareness by judicial operators still result in impunity for perpetrators and make it difficult for victims of human rights violations to access effective remedies and support. 8 Ibid., para. 3. 9 See www.ohchr.org/Documents/Issues/Discrimination/Joint_LGBTI_Statement_ENG.PDF. Consensual same-sex relationships remain a crime in 73 countries, which exposes individuals to the risk of arrest, blackmail and extortion, and feeds stigma, discrimination and violence. While five States have decriminalized homosexuality since 2011, in several other States new discriminatory law have been adopted or proposed, sanctions have been broadened and discriminatory restrictions placed on freedom of expression and association.10

Non-governmental and other sources provide a wealth of information and document a litany of abuses covering all parts of the globe.11 Underlying that panorama is the multifaceted nature of the violence and discrimination, which stretches from the home to the education system to the community setting to the State level and beyond. This is a systemic phenomenon, which will be discussed further below. V. Reflections

text: The entry point for the mandate holder is action against violence and discrimination. This is based on existing international human rights law and its interrelationship with sexual orientation and gender identity; there is no advocacy of new rights for particular groups.

text: Also important is the context-specific nature of each country and situation. The situation is not necessarily the same for lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender (and intersex) persons across the board, even though human rights are inherent to all persons without distinction: the situation is not homogeneous but heterogeneous. For instance, in one country, same-sex relationships are criminalized, with the threat of the death penalty. This is primarily targeted at homosexuals. However, in that same country, those who selfidentify as transgender are assisted and recognized by the State (to undergo reassignment surgery). The lack of awareness or understanding or knowledge, and the biases and stereotypes, vary between countries and within each country — depending on diverse factors such as geography (urban vs. rural), demography (e.g. different educational and economic levels), and cultural affinity.

text: The reflections that follow are an initial response regarding the key elements under the mandate. A. Implementation of international instruments, with identification of good practices and gaps

text: An array of international human rights instruments help to entrench calls for nonviolence and the principle of non-discrimination in international law, with due respect for sexual orientation and gender identity. The genesis of human rights protection after the Second World War was the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, of 1948. There are now nine core international human rights treaties, complemented by various protocols.12 All of them interrelate with the issue of sexual orientation and gender identity, to a lesser or greater extent. For instance, the right to be free from discrimination is propounded in article 2 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and in all human rights treaties. Article 2 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights stipulates: Each State Party to the present Covenant undertakes to respect and to ensure to all individuals within its territory and subject to its jurisdiction the rights recognized in 10 See Living Free and Equal, p. 11. 11 For example, a wealth of information was shared at the world conference of the International Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Trans and Intersex Association, held in Bangkok from 28 November to 2 December 2016; see http://ilga.org. The Independent Expert has begun attending a number of non-governmental conferences and thanks the hosts warmly for their kind hospitality. 12 See The Core International Human Rights Treaties (United Nations publication, Sales No.E.14.XIV.1). the present Covenant, without distinction of any kind, such as race, colour, sex, language, religion, political or other opinion, national or social origin, property, birth or other status.
committee: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity
committees: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity

text: Other provisions (e.g. article 7 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and article 26 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights) reaffirm the right to equality before the law and equal protection of the law without discrimination. The stricture against discrimination was deliberated upon by the Human Rights Committee in regard to a seminal case, Toonen v. Australia, that concerned the presence of a local law that prohibited same-sex relations. The Committee found that the local law in question violated article 17 of the Covenant in regard to the right to privacy, and that the reference to “sex” in article 2 (1) (as well as in art. 26) covered sexual orientation.13

committees: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity

text: Under the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, the monitoring committee has affirmed that the right to non-discrimination guaranteed by the Covenant includes sexual orientation, gender identity and sex characteristics. Under the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women and the Convention on the Rights of the Child, the monitoring committees have issued general comments and have made recommendations to States covering respect for sexual orientation and gender identity.

committees: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity

text: All countries have engaged with the Human Rights Council’s universal periodic review and most have engaged with one or more of the special procedures. There has been much coverage of the issue of sexual orientation and gender identity under these mechanisms, particularly from the angle of anti-violence and anti-discrimination, such as in the work of the Special Rapporteur on extrajudicial, summary or arbitrary executions and the Special Rapporteur on the right of everyone to the enjoyment of the highest attainable standard of physical and mental health.

committees: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity

text: As evidenced by the wide range of international human rights treaties that are in force, international human rights bodies and procedures — ranging from the human rights treaty bodies, with their general comments and recommendations, to the universal periodic review, to the special procedures’ coverage of sexual orientation and gender identity-related violations, to resolutions and studies — the international human rights system has been strengthening the promotion and protection of human rights without distinction. The protection of persons based on their sexual orientation and gender identity, and the mandate of the Independent Expert, are based on international law, complemented and supplemented by State practice.

committees: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity

text: Action against violence and discrimination has been espoused more recently in the 17 globally agreed Sustainable Development Goals, to which all countries are committed, with a framework of 2015-2030 for operationalization. Goal 16, which covers inclusive societies and access to justice, aims to bring about substantial reductions of violence and to promote anti-discrimination measures, on the basis of leaving no one behind. An allinclusive approach invites effective coverage of all persons whatever their sexual orientation or gender identity.
committee: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity
committees: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity

text: The initiatives of regional organizations have led to constructive developments. The European human rights system has evolved greatly and proactively on the issue of sexual orientation and gender identity. The Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (European Convention on Human Rights) has flourished, with important case work on sexual orientation and gender identity being carried out. Furthermore, a number of articles of the Convention, on such matters as the right to nondiscrimination, the prohibition of torture, the right to privacy and the right to freedom of expression have been the subject of judicial deliberation. There have been a variety of cases before the European Court of Human Rights, covering a wide expanse of Europe and 13 See communication No. 488/1992, Views adopted on 31 March 1994. There have been many other cases, for example Young v. Australia and X v. Colombia, concerning discrimination on the grounds of sex or sexual orientation: see communications No. 941/2000, Views adopted on 6 August 2003, and No. 1361/2005, Views adopted on 30 March 2007, respectively. interlinking geographically with the furthest reaches of Asia, with much innovative thinking.14 In parallel to this, the European Union, with its Charter of Fundamental Rights, has strengthened measures against violence and discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity, including via the collection and collation of data through the European Union Agency for Fundamental Rights to inform policymaking and action.15
committee: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity
committees: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity

text: The inter-American system has offered many contributions to action against violence and discrimination. In addition to its important range of human rights-related declarations and conventions and its regional human rights court and commission, it has appointed a regional rapporteur specifically to cover the issue of lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender and intersex persons. The General Assembly of the Organization of American States recently approved two treaties which refer to sexual orientation and gender identity directly as grounds on which discrimination must be prohibited: namely the Inter-American Convention Against All Forms of Discrimination and Intolerance and the Inter-American Convention on Protecting the Human Rights of Older Persons.16
committee: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity
committees: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity

text: Complementing the measures outlined above, resolution 275 of the African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights, on protection against violence and other human rights violations against persons on the basis of their real or imputed sexual orientation or gender identity, of 2014, resonates with the following message for the African region and beyond: Strongly urges States to end all acts of violence and abuse, whether committed by State or non-State actors, including by enacting and effectively applying appropriate laws prohibiting and punishing all forms of violence including those targeting persons on the basis of their imputed or real sexual orientation or gender identities, ensuring proper investigation and diligent prosecution of perpetrators, and establishing judicial procedures responsive to the needs of victims.17
committee: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity
committees: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity

text: Interregional cooperation bore fruit when the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights, the African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights and the United Nations held a joint dialogue in 2016, calling for more mainstreaming of regional and international norms to counter violence and discrimination, interlinking with the opportunities offered by the Sustainable Development Goals. The joint dialogue acknowledged positive steps from the African region, as follows: African States are almost all characterized by great diversity in their populations, with ethnic, religious and cultural diversity being the common denominator. In line with article 28 of the Charter,18 which calls on every individual “to respect and consider his fellow beings without discrimination, and to maintain relations aimed at promoting, safeguarding and reinforcing mutual respect and tolerance”, the Commission may advocate for the rights of all persons, including LGBT and intersex persons. In this respect, it can build on positive examples of State action in Africa and elsewhere to respect diversity and protect the human rights of all persons, irrespective of sexual orientation and gender identity. Participants noted that at least 19 African States do not criminalize consensual same-sex relations between adults in their legal systems, that Mozambique in 2014 removed criminal sanctions for such 14 See www.coe.int/en/web/sogi;and Frédéric Edel, Case Law of the European Court of Human Rights Relating to Discrimination on Grounds of Sexual Orientation or Gender Identity (Strasbourg, Council of Europe, 2015). 15 See, for example, European Union Agency for Fundamental Rights, EU LGBT survey - European Union lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender survey – Main results (Vienna, 2014), at http://fra.europa.eu/en/publication/2014/eu-lgbt-survey-european-union-lesbian-gay-bisexual-andtransgender-survey-main. 16 Ending Violence and Other Human Rights Violations Based on Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity: A Joint Dialogue of the African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights, Inter-American Commission on Human Rights and United Nations (Pretoria University Law Press, 2016), p. 62. See www.ohchr.org/Documents/Issues/Discrimination/Endingviolence_ACHPR_IACHR_UN_SOGI_dial ogue_EN.pdf. 17 Ibid., p. 28. 18 African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights. conduct, that Rwanda and other States have resisted recent attempts to introduce such laws into their legal system, that seven States prohibit discrimination in employment on the basis of sexual orientation, that courts in Botswana and Kenya, among others, recently declared the refusal to register LGBT associations to be unconstitutional, and that a number of national human rights institutions (including in Kenya, Uganda and South Africa) have expressed themselves against human rights violations based on sexual orientation or gender identity.19

committees: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity

text: Other regional human rights instruments offer opportunities for advocacy against violence and discrimination. For instance, it is stated in the Arab Charter on Human Rights, of 2004, in its article 3, that: Each State party to the present Charter undertakes to ensure to all individuals subject to its jurisdiction the right to enjoy the rights and freedoms set forth herein, without distinction on grounds of race, colour, sex, language, religious belief, opinion, thought, national or social origin, wealth, birth or physical or mental disability.20

committees: IE Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity

text: The ASEAN Human Rights Declaration, of 2012, stipulates that: Every person is entitled to the rights and freedoms set forth herein, without distinction of any kind, such as race, gender, age, language, religion, political or other opinion, national or social origin, economic status, birth, disability or other status.21
